narrative:
Your situation has been carefully reviewed, and the model estimates that you have a 17% chance of not completing the final year successfully. That means that, out of every hundred students with a similar profile, about seventeen would fail. Because this risk is seen as too high, you are required to take remedial courses to strengthen your foundation.

What is important to understand is that the most influential factors in your case are actually working in your favor. The single strongest factor is your record of past failures: you have none, which is exactly the same as the average student who passes. This pushes strongly toward a pass. The second most influential factor is your father’s education. He has completed higher education, while only about a quarter of students who pass have a father at that level. That also points toward success. The third factor is your own desire to pursue higher education. In the data, every single student who passed wanted to go on to higher education, so your “yes” is a positive sign.

So why are you being asked to take remedial courses? Because, after weighing all the other details of your situation together, the model still sees a meaningful chance of failure. These three strong positives are not enough to lower the risk below the required threshold. This doesn’t mean you will fail, but it does mean extra preparation would be wise. Consider building on your study habits, staying engaged in your courses, and making use of available academic support so that the positive signals in your profile are fully reflected in your final results.
